latin.706: §. IV. Equidem videntur quandoque Patres opinari, etiam indignos corporis Christi fieri participes, sed id inde evenit, quòd metonymicè loquuntur Patres, Sacramentum corporis Christi, seu panem Domini, ad exemplum Christi ipsius, corpus Christi haud rarò nuncupantes.
latin.707: Hinc Picherellus Pontificius: Ceterum, inquit, Patrum metonymica locutiones occasionem multis præbuêre, cur & indignos crederent corpus Christi manducare.
latin.708: Et postquam Augustini, aliorumque Patrum nonnulla hujusmodi testimonia recitasset, pergit: Obsecro Te, nonne ex his testimoniis, infideles & Indigni videntur Christi vesci corpore? At verò ipsum jam audiamus Augustinum, se suámque Metonymiam interpretantem.
latin.709: Quum, quod corpus, sive carnem & sanguinem Christi hic dicit, alibi, in non dissimili sententia, exponens, in Joan. tract. 27. appellat carnem Christi, & sanguinem Christi in sacramento, in Johan. 26. & ad Inquisit. Januarii cap. 3. Sacramentum corporis & sanguinis, de Eccles. Dogmat. cap. 53. Eucharistiam: & quod etiam de Juda quoque, unáque reliquis Apostolis, dicit in Psal. 10. interpretatur Eucharistiam primùm confectam in Johan. cap. 12. & contra Donat. post. Coll. cap. 6. panem, & in Johan. tract. 59. panem Domini, non panem Dominum, in Psal. 3. Corporis sui figuram, contra Adamant. cap. 12. Corporis sui signum, de verbo Domini secundum Matth. Serm. 11. Sacramentum Carnis & Sanguinis primùm confectum, de verbo Domini secundum Lucam. serm. 33. Cœnam manibus suis consecratam.
latin.710: Ad inquis. Januar. ad eum modum cum dixisset, liquido apparet quum primùm acceperunt discipuli corpus & sanguinem Domini, non eos accepisse jejunos, paulo post, loco corporis & sanguinis Domini ponit Sacramentum: neque enim, inquit, quia post cibos dedit Dominus, propterea pransi aut cænati, fratres ad illud Sacramentum accipiendum, venire debent. En metonymiam explicatam, figuratámque, in propriam reductam locutionem pag. 181. & 182.
latin.711: Reliquorum Patrum figuratas hujusmodi sententias, simili interpretatione donat Picherellus loc. cit., à pag. 182. in med. ad finem usque Capitis sui tertii, in cujus initio exponit, quid Pronomen HOC, in dicto Christi, Hoc est corpus meum, demonstret, à pag. 163.

pass_a.706: §. IV. Indeed the Fathers sometimes seem to opine that even the unworthy become partakers of Christ’s body, but that happens because the Fathers speak metonymically, not rarely naming the Sacrament of Christ’s body, or the bread of the Lord, Christ’s body — after Christ’s own example.
pass_a.707: Hence Picherellus the Pontifician: Moreover, he says, the Fathers’ metonymic locutions afforded many occasion why they should believe even the unworthy eat Christ’s body.
pass_a.708: And after he had recited some such testimonies of Augustine and of other Fathers, he continues: I beseech you, do not the unfaithful and Unworthy seem from these testimonies to feed on Christ’s body? But now let us hear Augustine himself interpreting himself and his Metonymy.
pass_a.709: When what he here calls body, or flesh and blood of Christ, elsewhere in a not unlike sense he exposits — in Tract. on John 27 he calls flesh of Christ and blood of Christ in the sacrament; in John 26 and to Januarius’s Inquiries ch. 3 Sacrament of body and blood; On Ecclesiastical Dogmas ch. 53 Eucharist; and what he also says of Judas with the remaining Apostles in Psalm 10 he interprets as the Eucharist first confected (John 12); and against the Donatists post Coll. ch. 6 bread; and in Tract. on John 59 bread of the Lord, not bread the Lord; in Psalm 3 figure of his Body; against Adamantius ch. 12 sign of his Body; on the Lord’s word according to Matthew Serm. 11 Sacrament of Flesh and Blood first confected; on Luke serm. 33 the Supper consecrated by his own hands.
pass_a.710: To Januarius’s Inquiries, after he had spoken in that manner, it clearly appears that when the disciples first received the Lord’s body and blood they did not receive fasting — a little later, in place of the Lord’s body and blood he puts Sacrament: for neither, he says, because the Lord gave after meals should brethren therefore come breakfasted or suppered to receive that Sacrament. Behold the metonymy explained, and the figured speech reduced to proper locution, pp. 181–182.
pass_a.711: Picherellus at the cited place grants like interpretation to the remaining Fathers’ figured sentences of this kind, from p. 182 mid to the end of his third Chapter — at whose beginning he exposits what the Pronoun THIS demonstrates in Christ’s saying, This is my body, from p. 163.

706: §.IV: the Fathers sometimes seem to teach that even the unworthy partake Christ’s body.
That appearance comes from metonymy — they often call the sacrament or the Lord’s bread “Christ’s body,” following Christ’s own speech.
707: The Fathers’ metonymic turns gave many occasion to believe the unworthy eat Christ’s body.
708: After listing Augustine and other Fathers in that vein, Picherellus asks: don’t the unfaithful and unworthy seem, from these texts, to feed on Christ’s body?
Answer: hear Augustine interpret his own metonymy.
709: What Augustine calls body (or flesh and blood) he elsewhere glosses as flesh and blood in the sacrament, as sacrament of body and blood, as Eucharist.

Of Judas with the Apostles he means the Eucharist first made — bread, bread of the Lord not bread the Lord, figure and sign of his body, the sacrament first confected, the supper consecrated by his hands.
710: In Ad Inquis. Januarii he says the disciples first received “body and blood” not fasting — then swaps in “sacrament”: they need not come already fed to that sacrament.
So the figure is reduced to proper speech (pp. 181–182).
711: Picherellus reads the other Fathers’ figured lines the same way through the end of his third chapter.
He also opens what THIS points to in “This is my body” (from p. 163). Stop §.IV before §.V (Classis III Rationativa).
